description:
During the 2026 Legislative Session, the City of Daytona Beach Shores successfully secured a $375,000 state appropriation for the purchase of mobile stormwater infrastructure equipment. The appropriation was supported by Senator Tom Wright and Representative Chase Tramont and approved as part of the State's Fiscal Year 2026–2027 budget.
The funding is being administered through the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) under Grant Agreement L0439.
The appropriation will assist the City in purchasing a combination jet/vacuum truck (VacCon or equivalent) to remove sand, debris, and other obstructions from stormwater drainage systems. This equipment will enhance the City's ability to perform preventative maintenance, address localized flooding, and respond more effectively to severe weather events.
The grant agreement provides $375,000 in state funding on a reimbursement basis, with no matching requirement imposed by FDEP. The equipment must be purchased by December 31, 2027, and the agreement expires June 30, 2028.

description:
The 2026 Daytona Beach Shores Vulnerability Assessment, funded in part through the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's Resilient Florida Program, evaluates the City's vulnerability to flooding, storm surge, sea-level rise, and other water-related hazards in accordance with Section 380.093, Florida Statutes. The assessment evaluated roadways, critical infrastructure, community and emergency facilities, and other assets using current conditions and future projections for 2040 and 2070.
The assessment identifies storm surge as a significant vulnerability due largely to the City's barrier-island location between the Atlantic Ocean and Halifax River Lagoon. Under the current-day Category 5 storm scenario, 100% of the critical assets and roadways evaluated are impacted by flooding, with future projections indicating increased flooding and flood depths.
The report recommends using the assessment to guide future capital improvements, stormwater planning, hazard mitigation, land-use decisions, resilient infrastructure improvements, and pursuit of state and federal funding. Potential strategies include floodproofing or elevating critical facilities, stormwater improvements, green infrastructure, resilient redevelopment, and incorporating climate projections into future planning.
Overall, the assessment provides the City with a planning tool to identify and prioritize vulnerable infrastructure and future resilience investments. Individual recommendations remain subject to future City decisions, available funding, and implementation capacity.
title: Resolution 2026-13 Adopting of the Vulnerability Assessment presented by East Central Florida Regional Planning Council

description:
February 28, 2023 City Commission approved Resolution 2023-04 Fund Balance Policy setting minimum balances for the General Fund unrestricted fund balance and the Enterprise Fund (Sewer) unrestricted fund balance. The General Fund was set at 50% of the current year's budgeted ad valorem tax revenues. The Enterprise Fund was set to 50% of budgeted revenues.
What makes up fund balance: inventories and prepaid items, restricted funds for law enforcement, road improvements, & domestic abuse, assigned funds for capital projects and subsequent year's budget, and unassigned funds. Unassigned funds are the funds able to be used for emergency purchases, purchases that come up throughout the year that are not in the budget, capital, and other programs. A fund balance policy sets limits to the minimums the city should have. The current policy sets the General Fund unassigned funds at the minimum of 50% of budgeted ad valorem tax revenue. Current budgeted ad valorem tax revenue is $10,430,400. That would mean the city would need to have $5,215,200 in unassigned funds for FY 25-26. At FYE 24-25 the city had $18,786,147. Currently, the city has $17,275,743 in unassigned funds. This meets the policy minimums.
What makes up net position: net investment in capital assets, restricted funds for sewer impact fees, and unrestricted funds. Unrestricted funds are available for emergency purchases, purchases that come up throughout the year that are not budgeted for, and capital. The current fund balance policy sets the Enterprise Fund unrestricted funds balance at 50% of the current year's budgeted revenues. The current budgeted operating revenues for the Enterprise Fund are $43,674,800. This amount includes grants, charges for service, interest, and debt proceeds. According to the fund balance policy the Enterprise Fund should have $21,837,400 in unrestricted funds. The Enterprise Fund had $12,498,839 in unrestricted funds at FYE 24-25 and currently has $12,236,839 in unrestricted funds. This is $9.6 million less than what the fund balance policy states.This highlights the discrepancy in using operating revenues as the deciding factor. It is staff recommendation to utilize 50% of the prior year's total charges for service. If this amount was used, the minimum balance would be $1,946,305 as charges for services totaled $3,892,610.(2024-25 ACFR). This amount is more inline with what the minimum should be, especially with the increase in capital projects within the sewer fund.

description:
The 2853 S. Atlantic Avenue site (n/k/a St. Kitts Park) originated from a developer agreement associated with a rezoning approval considered by the City Council on August 28, 2002. At that meeting, the City approved a rezoning and a future land use map amendment for the property located along South Atlantic Avenue.
As part of the approval, the property owner agreed to convey a portion of the site, specifically the northern 40 feet, to the City for use as a public park upon completion of the development .
This action resulted in the City obtaining the property in March 2005, at no cost and ensured that the development included a public benefit in the form of park land.
The Parks and Recreation Master Plan approved by the City Commission on September 23, 2025, identifies St. Kitts Park as the #2 priority capital improvement project based on system-wide needs and community input.
Key factors supporting this ranking include:
Demand for additional neighborhood parks and passive recreation opportunities
Need for increased shade, walkability, and accessible green space
Identified gap in park access within the surrounding residential area
Consistency with system priorities, including:Neighborhood-scale parks
Passive recreation amenities
Enhanced landscaping and tree canopy
Community gathering spaces
Public input received during the master planning process indicated strong usage of existing parks, along with a need for additional neighborhood-level facilities. Residents also expressed interest in trails, shaded areas, and walkable park spaces.
The St. Kitts Park site ranked highly due to its location within a residential area, its suitability for low-impact daily use, its relatively low development cost, and its ability to improve equitable access to park facilities.
On April 7, 2026, City Commission approved a contract with Zev Cohen Engineering to design and engineer the park in order for staff to apply for a Volusia County ECHO grant to help fund the project.

The City of Daytona Beach Shores seeks City Commission approval to apply for the Technical Assistance Panel (TAP) program through the Urban Land Institute and to appropriate $25,000 from general reserves to support participation in the program.
Daytona Beach Shores is a coastal community that has historically functioned as a pass-through corridor rather than a destination with a defined downtown or community core. As the City looks to evolve into a vibrant, walkable coastal destination, several challenges remain, including the absence of a clearly defined downtown or gateway, auto-oriented corridors such as Dunlawton Boulevard, and the presence of underutilized and aging properties—particularly in the northwest area of the City. Additional constraints include fragmented property ownership and development regulations that may not fully support mixed-use, pedestrian-oriented environments.
Despite these challenges, the City is well-positioned for transformation. The emerging Civic Hub and municipal campus, along with increasing private sector interest, including projects like the Aston Martin Residences, present a unique opportunity to establish a strong town center and attract high-quality development.
Participation in the ULI TAP program would provide independent, expert guidance in planning, urban design, economic development, and implementation strategies. The panel will help the City address key questions related to defining a downtown or gateway area, stimulating redevelopment and investment, and identifying policy and regulatory changes needed to support long-term revitalization.

description:
The Truth in Millage (TRIM) process informs taxpayers, and the public, about the legislative process local taxing authorities use to determine ad valorem property, taxes. This process is governed by Florida State Statute Chapter 200 and provides for public input and requires each taxing authority to provide specific reasons for any changes in taxes and annual budget. The process begins with the property appraiser delivering an estimate of the total assessed value of nonexempt property to the City Manager and Finance Director of Daytona Beach Shores. This value is used for budget planning purposes.
Department directors, along with the City Manager and the Finance Director, meet regularly to develop a budget that delivers all the services, along with the personnel and equipment needed to deliver the services residents come to expect from their city. A workshop, open to residents, with staff and commission is scheduled in July where the proposed budget is presented. The Finance Director will highlight the changes in the budget from the prior year emphasizing increases in costs, and capital purchases. This is the time for residents and commissioners to discuss the budget: costs, effects on millage rate, items that should be added or subtracted, or anything having to do with the annual city budget. The budget workshop for FY 26-27 can be held either on Tuesday, July 21st at 4:00 pm with a special commission meeting to follow at 6:00 pm to accept a proposed millage rate or on Tuesday, July 28th at 4:00 pm with a special commission meeting to follow at 6:00 pm. Proposed millage rates must be submitted to the Volusia County Property Appraiser no later than August 4, 2026.
After the property appraiser receives the proposed millage rate from all municipalities, they will send out, to all property owners, the Notice of Proposed Property Tax. This is usually around August 24th.
Note: Once the proposed millage rate is approved, the city cannot approve a rate higher than the proposed rate without re-advertising the new rate to all property owners.
The City of Daytona Beach Shores must hold two public hearings during the budget process. The first or tentative hearing for the FY 26-27 Budget will be advertised in the Notice of Proposed Property Tax. Hearings must be scheduled between September 3rd and September 18th after 5:00 pm. Volusia County cannot schedule its hearings on days the school board has hearings scheduled and municipalities are not able to hold public hearings on the same days as Volusia County or Volusia County School Board. This is to allow tax payers the ability to attend each budget hearing. Volusia County is scheduled to have their first budget hearing on September 3rd and the School Board is scheduled for September 8th. The city can reschedule its normal monthly meeting from Tuesday, September 1st to Wednesday, September 9th to incorporate the first budget hearing. The meeting would be at the usual 6:00 pm time.
The second, and final public hearing can be scheduled between September 18th and October 4th. The city can schedule a special commission meeting on Tuesday, September 22th at 6:00 pm to discuss and approve the final millage rate and budget.
At each public hearing the percentage increase in millage over the rolled-back rate needed to fund the budget must be discussed along with the reason for any increase in ad valorem tax revenues. The rolled-back rate is the rate that will generate the same revenue as the prior year. These hearings are the opportunity for residents, staff, and commissioners to discuss the city's FY 26-27 Budget.

description:
The city applied for a Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) grant in August 2023, after hurricanes Ian and Nicole. The city felt it necessary to construct an Emergency Operations Center (EOC) as city staff were stationed at several city buildings throughout the storms. The grant consisted of two phases; Phase 1 Assessment, Engineering, Surveying, and Permitting at a cost of $439,425 and Phase 2 Construction at a cost of $3,558,345 for a 2,400 square foot facility to be positioned between the Public Safety building and the fleet building. At the time of application and contract execution, it was understood the city would be responsible for 25% of the project and the grant would cover the remaining 75%.
The city was granted Phase 1 of the application with the anticipation that, if Phase 1 deliverables were approved, Phase 2, construction, would be approved. Commission approved the Phase 1 contract at the March 4th commission meeting. The contract was signed and returned to the Florida Department of Emergency Management, (FDEM) who administers the grant program for Federal Emergency Management Assistance (FEMA). The city received a fully executed contract on March 31, 2025 and was able to begin the procurement process. The contract award date, beginning date, was October 14, 2024, 5.5 months prior to the city receiving a fully executed contract and the approval to move forward with procurement. The city prepared bid documents to hire an architectural engineer for Phase 1. The Commission approved staff's recommendation for an engineer at the September 8, 2025 meeting. The initial meeting with staff and the engineer was on October 9th to go over the scope of work and schedule. It was noted the contract performance period end date was January 31, 2026, 3.5 months from the scope meeting. It was determined staff would have to request an extension from FDEM as the estimated time frame for the engineering would be, at best, 9-10 months.
Staff contacted FDEM and submitted the necessary paperwork for the extension request. It was relayed from FDEM that the entire project, including Phase 2 would have to be completed and closed out by June 20, 2028 with no extensions possible. That would mean Phase 1 and Phase 2, construction would need to be completed prior to the close of the grant on June 20 2028; 28.5 months of which 10 would be for engineering and then the time for the city to approve the deliverables along with FDEM and to get approval for Phase 2. This would leave approximately 16 months to construct the EOC. It was also conveyed the cost share of the project was 60/40, not the original 75/25 originally ​anticipated.
Staff looked at the timeline for the project, ​the estimated increase in cost, the change in cost ​share, and the highly motivated conversations around property tax elimination, the city being 82% residential property, and determined it ​may be best for the city to withdraw from the EOC project at this time.
​

description:
House Bill 7073 adopted in 2024 provides taxing authorities, such as the City of Daytona Beach Shores, the option to opt-out of the Live Local Act tax exemption for certain moderate income affordable new housing units rented to households who earn between 80-120% of the Area Median Income (AMI) for the Volusia Metropolitian Statistical Area (MSA), provided a surplus of affordable housing for the category entitled “0-120 percent AMI" exists. This "opt-out" provision is now codified in Section 196.1978(3)(o), Florida Statutes.
While other aspects of the Live Local Act are preempted from local authority, including certain land use and zoning decisions, the City of Daytona Beach Shores would not lose tax revenues from the aforementioned tax exemption by adopting Resolution 2025-23. Opting out of this exemption is for one year only and as such, local governments must renew annually and forward the resolution to the County Property Appraiser by January 1 of each year, providing the qualifying local conditions in Section 196.1978(3)(o), Florida Statutes are met. Per Section 196.1978(3)(o)(2), Florida Statutes, to qualify to "opt-out" of this exemption, the local government must rely on data from the most recent Shimberg Center for Housing Studies Annual Report.
The 2024 Shimberg Center for Housing Studies Annual Report demonstrated that Volusia MSA had a surplus of affordable housing for the category entitled “0-120 percent AMI" in 2024 and consequently, the city elected to opt out as provided by law. The 2025 Shimberg Center for Housing Studies Annual Report is yet to be published. Therefore, Resolution 2025-23 is crafted such that the resolution does not become effective unless the 2025 Shimberg Report demonstrates a surplus of affordable housing in the Volusia MSA as required by law.

Term Limits: Termed out members shall sit out at least one full three-year term.

description:
Pursuant to Section 163.3191(1), Florida Statutes, at least once every seven (7) years, local governments are required to evaluate and appraise their land use comprehensive plan to determine if plan amendments are necessary to reflect changes in state requirements since the last update of the comprehensive plan and notify the state land planning agency as to its determination. The resultant document produced after this process, which may have proposed comprehensive plan amendments, is called the Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR).
On February 4, 2025, the City Commission of the City of Daytona Beach Shores approved Ordinance 2025-01 on first reading, which resulted in the transmittal of a series of EAR-based comprehensive plan amendments to the Florida Department of Commerce (FDC) and other state agencies in accordance with Sec. 163.3191(2), Florida Statutes, for a state coordinate review per Sec. 163.3184(4), Florida Statutes. On April 18, 2025, the FDC provided their Objections, Recommendations and Comments (ORC) Report regarding the proposed plan amendments. The FDC ORC Report contained one objection and two comments, all of which have been addressed in this adoption package/ordinance.
Ordinance 2025-01, if adopted, amends the Comprehensive Plan Update (2030) by making the following changes (Exhibit A).
Extend the comprehensive plan planning horizon to the year 2045.
Chapter 1-Future Land Use Element: (a) Minor Housecleaning text amendments, including, but not limited to, references to the new planning horizon. (b) Policy 1-1.4.2: Including off-beach parking lots as a permitted use in the Public/Quasi-Public Land Use Category. (c) Update Future Land Use Element map series to account for the revised planning period and past updates. The Future Land Use Element map series includes: (1) Map L-1, Existing Land Use; (2) Map L-2, Coastal High Hazard Area Map; (3) Map L-3, Generalized Adjacent Existing Land Uses; and (4) Map L-4, Future Land Use.
Chapter 2-Transportation Element: (a) Update the Transportation Element map series to account for the revised planning period and past updates. The Transportation Element map series includes: (1) Map 2-1, Major Thoroughfares by Functional Classification; (2) Map 2-2, Significant Traffic Generators and Attractions; (3) Map 2-3, Future Transit Facilities and Pedestrian/Bikeways; (4) Map 2-4, Level of Service; and (5) Map 2-5, Hurricane Evacuation Routes. (b) Minor Housecleaning text amendments.
Chapter 4-Public Facilities Element: (a) Update Policy 4-1.3.10 “Daytona Beach Shores Water Supply Facilities Work Plan” to reflect a new planning horizon and update data consistent with population and water demand projections and the City’s water providers’ respective water supply facilities work plans per Sec. 163.3177(6)(c)4-5, Florida Statutes. (b) Create new Objective 4-1.7 and respective policies to address Sec. 163.3177(6)(c)3, Florida Statutes, regarding sanitary sewer feasibility study requirements for developments with greater than 50 residential lots not connected to the City’s sanitary sewer system.
Chapter 5-Coastal Management Element: (a) Minor Housecleaning text amendments. (b) Policy 5-1.1.1: Amend policy to remove outdated community redevelopment area off beach parking reference and replace with commitment to maintain existing city off-beach parking spaces. (c) Policy 5-1.3.1: Amend policy to promote the development of a beach management plan that accounts for long-term community resiliency and the protection of uplands. (d) Policy 5-1.7.4: Update the sanitary sewer, solid waste and potable water level of service standards consistent with the City of Port Orange. (e) Policy 5-1.11.1: Update to include increase in boat slips subject to additional boat slip entitlements via the voluntary annexation process per Sec. 171.044, Florida Statutes.
Chapter 9-Capital Improvements Element: (a) Update the Daytona Beach Shores 5-Year Capital Improvement Plan per Sec. 163.3177(3)(b), Florida Statutes. (b) Update the Volusia County School District Five-Year Work Program per the Volusia County School District Interlocal Agreement. description:
This grant was applied for in August 2023 after Hurricane's Ian and Nicole devastated our area. The purpose of this Hurricane Nicole Hazard Mitigation Grant is to provide protection to three lift stations in Daytona Beach Shores.
The grant is funded through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) DR-4680-060-R, as approved by the Florida Division of Emergency Management (Division) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). The project is for the purchase and installation of an emergency system to reduce and/or mitigate damage that might otherwise occur from severe weather or other hazards.
The HMGP project shall provide backup power for Lift Station 7 with a 200-kW portable diesel generator; Lift Station 9 with a 56 kW permanent generator including a new concrete pad, 200-gallon subbase diesel fuel tank, and automatic transfer switching gear; and Lift Station 10 with a 100-kW portable diesel generator. The generators shall be of an adequate size determined by the vendor or electrical engineer during the bid process to appropriately support the lift stations. Lift Station 7, 9, and 10 do not have backup power .During previous storms these lift stations have lost power requiring the use of emergency bypass pumps powered by portable generators. Without power, these lift stations may experience backing up and sewage overflow leading to water and soil contamination as well as private property damage. Having backup power for these three lift stations will prevent overflows and will protect the health and safety of residents in the community

description:
The City posted an invitation to bid for the resurfacing of clay Tennis Courts 1 through 5 at the Daytona Beach Shores Community Center located at 3000 Bellemead Drive. The tennis courts have not been resurfaced since their construction in 2017. The industry standard for clay court resurfacing is every 3-4 years. City staff maintenance protocols, frequency of play and limited environmental stress have extended the lift and utility of the city tennis courts. However, it is now time to resurface all courts in order to maintain a high quality tennis play.
The original bid specs for resurfacing the tennis courts was drafted prior to Hurricane Milton in October of 2024. During Milton some clay was lost from the playing surfaces. Therefore, the invitation to bid was amended to invite bidders to provide additional clay material on the courts.
The bids received are as follows:J Courts, Inc: Resurfacing the five courts without additional hurricane loss clay: $49,500. Resurfacing the five courts with additional clay lost due to Hurricane Milton: $77,900. Resurfacing all six tennis courts with additional clay lost during Milton: $97,900.
Fast Dry Courts, Inc.: Resurfacing the five courts without additional hurricane loss clay: $61,594. Resurfacing the five courts with additional clay lost due to Hurricane Milton: $87,550. No bid was provided for resurfacing all courts, including Court 5.
Sport Surfaces, LLC: Resurfacing the five courts without additional hurricane loss clay: $471,250. No bids were provided for resurfacing the five courts with additional clay lost due to Hurricane Milton nor resurfacing all courts, including Court 5.
On April 15, 2025, the staff selection committee unanimously recommended approval of the J Courts, Inc. proposal to include the resurfacing of all six tennis courts with the additional clay that was lost due to Hurricane Milton for a total cost of $97,900. When the FY2024-2025 Budget was approved in September 2024, $70,000 was allocated for this project. Therefore, the additional $27,900 will be utilized from cost savings from other approved budgeted projects already completed and projects eliminated from this fiscal year.
The selection committee consisted of the City Manager, Community Services Director, Deputy Public Works Director and Streets/Parks Supervisor. The City Clerk's minutes of the meeting are attached. Staff has verified the J Courts, Inc. listed references and confirmed their experience and expertise for the job.
title: Approval of Tennis Courts Clay Resurfacing Project Independent Contractor's Agreement: J Courts, Inc.

The Hazard Mitigation Grant Program is administered by FEMA and supports governments in implementing projects that reduce the risk of future disasters. Volusia County has been allotted $43.5 million in funding for projects. Projects are funded 75/25 with the city having a 25% match.
The city is applying for HMGP funding for the sewer improvements and retrofit north of Dunlawton sewer project. The city has also applied for other funding for this project in anticipation of the project getting fully funded.

The city has had all sewer infrastructure assessed and GIS mapped. It was determined that 70 of the 350 manholes and 68,400’ of the 72,000 feet of sewer line require repairs/upgrades. Manholes will be raised or relocated to protect against flooding events.

description:
Daytona Beach Shores Sewer Lift Station 5, located at 134 Chershire Road, is designed to operate with two submersible pumps, which were both installed in 2004. One of the pumps recently failed and was removed for diagnosis. The diagnosis revealed several issues with the pump, which would cost $102,244.28 to repair, whereas purchasing a new replacement pump would cost $129,777.43, plus freight (see attached quote from Stewart's Electric Motor Works, Inc).
KEY CONSIDERATIONSAlthough the station is currently operating with the one remaining pump, this is not efficient and can create long-term issues.
If the remaining pump fails, the lift station bypass pump may not be able to provide continued services as needed, leading to potential environmental and health issues.
Lift Station 5 is the second largest in the City, servicing S. Atlantic Avenue (2000 - 2900 block), Florida Shores Boulevard and other side streets.
The failed pump in question was installed in 2004.
The average life span of a submersible pump is 8–15 years.
The failed pump has been rebuilt multiple times previously and seen its useful life.
Pursuant to the emergency purchasing provisions of the Daytona Beach Shores procurement regulations, Ordinance 2023-13, Sec. 2-9(i)(2), Staff is recommending the City Commission approve the emergency purchase contract for the acquisition of a new pump Sewer Lift Station 5 and waive the normal bid process for this item as the following criteria are met:
Ordinance 2023-13, Sec. 2-9(i)(2), Emergency purchase. An emergency exemption occurs when: a) certain conditions might adversely affect the life, health, safety and welfare of City employees, or citizens of the City, Staff Comment: Criterion Met
b) when City property or equipment are endangered, Staff Comment: N/A
c) when it is necessary to maintain or restore vital services, or Staff Comment: Criterion Met
d) situations arise which may cause major financial impact to the City should immediate action not be taken. Staff Comment: Criterion Met
NOTE: This is a budgeted item.
title: Approval Of Emergency Purchase Contract For Sewer Lift Station 5 Submersible Pump

description:
Overnight parking of vehicles at City-owned properties, such as the Community Center, has impacted the City's ability to provide adequate parking during planned events. Additionally, vehicles that park long-term on City-owned properties create a hazard to community interests in safety, aesthetics, and cleanliness.
Ordinance 2025-05, if adopted, would amend the Daytona Beach Shores Code of Ordinances, Sec. 22-22, entitled "Conditions Permitting Impoundment," to allow the impoundment of any vehicle parked overnight on any city property without the prior approval of the City Manager, or designee. The Ordinance would also enact a new section 22-73, entitled "Overnight Parking on City-Owned Property," which would (1) prohibit overnight parking of vehicles on any city-owned or controlled property without the prior approval of the City Manager, or designee; and (2) establish that violations may result in vehicle impoundment.

description:
Resolution 2025-05, if adopted, will support and accept the Volusia County Multi-Jurisdictional Local Mitigation Strategy and the Volusia County Integrated Floodplain Management Plan. Both documents were drafted by the Volusia Prepares Working Group, of which the city is a member of, with the assistance of the East Central Florida Regional Planning Council.
The Federal Community Rating System/National Flood Insurance Program grades communities and reduces their flood insurance premiums providing certain parameters are met, such as having a Local Mitigation Strategy and Flood Management Plan. Local governments in Volusia County, including Daytona Beach Shores, have worked together to develop the referenced plans, which establish goals, objectives and projects that will reduce the potential for personal and public property losses in flood-prone areas, ensure the lowest possible flood insurance premiums for residents and save lives. Supporting and accepting the revised plans enable the City and other local governments in Volusia County to achieve the aforementioned goals.
title: Resolution 2025-05: Supporting And Accepting The Volusia County Local Mitigation Strategy Plan And Floodplain Management Plan

description:
The Daytona Beach Shores Volusia Growth Management Commission (VGMC) representative's term is scheduled to expire on June 30, 2025. Larry Saffer, former Code Enforcement Board Chair, has represented the City on VGMC since April 2016. The VGMC is requesting the City reappoint Mr. Saffer to the VGMC (see attached email). Mr. Saffer has indicated he would be willing to serve another term. If approved, the appointment would be for a four (4) year term.
The VGMC was established by the County of Volusia in 1986. "The main purpose of the commission is to provide an effective means for coordinating the plans of municipalities and the county, in order to provide a forum for the several local governments in the county to cooperate with each other in coordinating the provision of public services to and improvements for the citizens of the county, and create incentives to foster intergovernmental cooperation and coordination" (VGMC Website, 2025). The VGMC realizes this purpose by evaluating all comprehensive plan amendments submitted by local governments within the county and issues consistency certifications if the amendments do not negatively impact public infrastructure and other local government comprehensive plan policies.

Pursuant to Section 163.3191(1), Florida Statutes, at least once every seven (7) years, local governments are required to evaluate and appraise their land use comprehensive plan to determine if plan amendments are necessary to reflect changes in state requirements since the last update of the comprehensive plan and notify the state land planning agency as to its determination.
On March 12, 2024, the City of Daytona Beach Shores notified the state land planning agency, the Florida Department of Commerce (FDC), that the City intends to transmit the appropriate amendments in accordance with Sec. 163.3191(2), Florida Statutes.
City staff has completed review of the Daytona Beach Shores Comprehensive Plan Update (2030) relative to changes in state law since the 2017 adoption of the most recent Evaluation and Appraisal Report comprehensive plan amendments. Ordinance 2025-01, if adopted, amends the Comprehensive Plan Update (2030) by making the following changes (Exhibit A).
Extend the comprehensive plan planning horizon to the year 2045.
Chapter 1-Future Land Use Element: (a) Minor Housecleaning text amendments, including, but not limited to, references to the new planning horizon. (b) Policy 1-1.4.2: Including off-beach parking lots as a permitted use in the Public/Quasi-Public Land Use Category.
Chapter 5-Coastal Management Element: (a) Minor Housecleaning text amendments. (b) Policy 5-1.1.1: Amend policy to remove outdated community redevelopment area off beach parking reference and replace with commitment to maintain existing city off-beach parking spaces. (c) Policy 5-1.3.1: Amend policy to promote the development of a beach management plan that accounts for long-term community resiliency and the protection of uplands. (d) Policy 5-1.7.4: Update the sanitary sewer, solid waste and potable water level of service standards consistent with the City of Port Orange. (e) Policy 5-1.11.1: Update to include increase in boat slips subject to additional boat slip entitlements via the voluntary annexation process per Sec. 171.044, Florida Statutes.
Chapter 9-Capital Improvements Element: (a) Update the Daytona Beach Shores 5-Year Capital Improvement Plan per Sec. 163.3177(3)(b), Florida Statutes. (b) Update the Volusia County School District Five-Year Work Program per the Volusia County School District Interlocal Agreement. (c) Policy 9-1.3.1: Update the sanitary sewer, solid waste and potable water level of service standards consistent with the City of Port Orange.
Chapter 11-Public School Facilities Element: (a) Minor Housecleaning text amendments.
In accordance with Section 163.3191(2), Florida Statutes, the City is transmitting the plan amendments to the FDC and other state review agencies for a State Coordinated Review per Sec. 163.3184(4), Florida Statutes. Per Volusia Growth Management Commission (VGMC) Rules, the amendments will also be transmitted for VGMC review. The deadline for transmittal is March 12, 2024 (Exhibit B).

description:
Pursuant to Section 5-8 of the Daytona Beach Shores Land Development Code, the Daytona Beach Shores City Commission shall establish all permit fees by resolution or ordinance. Further, established fees shall be set forth in the current "City of Daytona Beach Shores Land Development Code Schedule of Fees."
The city's original Land Development Code Schedule of Fees was adopted in 1980 and has not been substantially updated since 1999. Resolution 2025-01, if adopted, would provide the first substantial building permit fee update in over 25 years and accomplish the following:
Simplify permit fee calculation method for building, electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing, signs, fences and expired permit re-instatement.
Increase the afore-stated building permit fees to become more comparable with other Volusia County coastal communities and reduce the revenue loss gap between cost of administering/enforcing Florida Building Codes and permit fees collected.
Align building permit re-inspection fees with Section 553.80.(2)(c), Florida Statutes.
Add private provider fee reductions, consistent with Section 553.791.(2)(b), Florida Statutes.

description: Hurricane Milton hit Volusia County on October 9 and 10 of 2024. Subsequent damage assessments conducted by City staff determined that several city public pedestrian beach access dune walkovers were damaged, including the walkover at 2901 S. Atlantic Avenue (Tuscany Shores). Upon further investigation, the city's structural engineering consultant recommended the Tuscany Shores dune walkover be completely replaced and determined that the structure is not in danger of imminent collapse on its own without an external force. This means that a storm or another external force could cause the imminent collapse of the Tuscany Shores public access dune walkover, which is bolted into the condominium's seawall. Consequently, city staff and condominium representatives have worked together to develop the subject agreement which, if approved, would authorize the city, to (1) remove the dune walkover from the seawall, (2) patch repair the seawall areas where the dune walkover bolts have been removed, and (3) paint said patched areas as articulated in the agreement.
